inline.s: [Immeasurable eons of life] The lifespan is vast and without bound (an arhat has already transcended birth and death). “Kuang” means extremely far-reaching. [Dwelling and moving through heaven and earth] Whether in the heavens or in the human world, one dwells and moves freely as one pleases.

blocks.text: Chapter 2: Severing Desire and Ending Pursuit

inline.s: The Buddha said: “A renunciant monk severs desire and abandons love, recognizes the source of his own mind, penetrates the profound principle of the Buddha, and awakens to the unconditioned Dharma. Within, there is nothing attained; without, nothing sought. The mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma. No thought, no doing; neither practice nor realization. Without passing through the stages, it is itself the supreme; this is called the Way.”

[Source of the mind] The mind is the root of all dharmas, hence “source of the mind.” The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says: “When a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it. When delusion subsides, the source of the mind is empty and still; all virtues are complete and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible.” The Calming and Contemplation (Zhiguan) says: “Sitting cross-legged with hands folded, sealing the lips and stilling the tongue, contemplating reality, when the source of the mind rests in a single point, the dharma-realm is equally still.” It also says: “If you wish to contemplate and know, you must know the source of the mind; the source of the mind is non-dual, and then all dharmas are the same as empty space.”

[Awakening to the unconditioned Dharma] The unconditioned Dharma spoken of here is exactly: “Within, there is nothing attained; without, nothing sought. The mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma. No thought, no doing; neither practice nor realization. Without passing through the stages, it is itself the supreme; this is called the Way.” It is the unconditioned Dharma of which the Diamond Sutra says, “All sages and saints differ through the unconditioned Dharma.” This is to “cultivate” in accordance with the ultimate truth — the reality of all dharmas. Although one cultivates the Way, one does not cling to the marks of the Way; therefore “within, there is nothing attained; without, nothing sought; the mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma; no thought, no doing; neither practice nor realization.” It is the sudden teaching that need not pass through the fifty-two stages but directly attains Buddhahood; hence it is said: “Without passing through the stages, it is itself the supreme; this is called the Way.” The Qing scholar Peng Jiqing praised: “This sutra embraces both the sudden and the gradual. First it declares, ‘Recognize the mind, reach the source, and understand the unconditioned Dharma, and be called a monk.’ Then it says, ‘The mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma; no thought, no doing; neither practice nor realization; without passing through the stages, it is itself the supreme; this is called the Way.’ The purport of non-dwelling in the Diamond Sutra and the door of non-duality in the Vimalakirti Sutra do not go beyond this!”

[The fifty-two stages] From a common person to Buddhahood, the Great Vehicle has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths (the “ten” indicates that it contains ten stages; likewise below), the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment (the Buddha fruit). [The mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma] The mind does not cling to the marks of cultivation, nor does it create karma.

blocks.text: Chapter 3: Cutting Off Love and Renouncing Greed

inline.s: The Buddha said: “One who shaves head and beard to become a monk and receives the Dharma of the Way renounces worldly wealth and asks only for enough alms. One meal a day, one night under a tree — take care not to seek more! What makes people deluded and dull are love and desire.”

Love and desire are the coarsest afflictions and obstacles of a cultivator. Greed, hatred, and delusion begin here; hence one creates karma, hence one receives retribution, hence one revolves in birth and death. To renounce love and desire and receive the Way — this is the crux of whether one can practice accordingly. Master Ouyi said: He praises the superior ascetic practices as the essential means of realizing the Way.

Cultivators of course all know the six realms of transmigration and the law of cause and effect, and that they themselves are on the bodhi path. But when they encounter circumstances and conditions, they are either deluded by external objects or drawn along by karmic bonds, and so they go against the Way. This is exactly what is meant by “What makes people deluded and dull are love and desire.”

The Lu Shi Chunqiu (The Spring and Autumn Annals of Mr. Lu) tells the story of “A man of Qi seizing gold”: A man of Qi desired to get gold. Early in the morning he put on his clothes and cap and went to the place where gold was sold. Seeing someone holding gold, he snatched it and seized it. The constable caught him, bound him, and asked: “Everyone is present here; why did you seize that man’s gold?” He replied: “I truly did not see the people — I only saw the gold.”

blocks.text: Chapter 4: Good and Evil Made Clear

inline.s: The Buddha said: “Living beings accomplish good through ten things, and likewise accomplish evil through ten things. What are the ten? Three of body, four of speech, three of mind. The three of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The four of speech are divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, and idle talk. The three of the mind are envy, anger, and delusion. These ten things, not following the holy path, are called the ten evil deeds. If these evils are stopped, they are called the ten good deeds.”

Practicing the ten wholesome courses of action is the basic virtue of a Buddhist, able to sever the suffering of the three evil realms (the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and the hell realm), and is the foundation for accomplishing a human body, a celestial body, and all holy fruits (arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, buddha).

blocks.text: Chapter 5: The Turning Point of Rise and Fall

inline.s: The Buddha said: “When a person has many faults and does not repent of them, but abruptly stills his mind, the offenses come upon his body, as water returns to the sea, gradually growing deep and vast. If a person has faults, understands them and recognizes his error, reforms evil and practices good, the offenses naturally vanish, as a sick person who sweats gradually recovers.”

A person has all kinds of faults yet does not know enough to repent, so as to abruptly still the mind that does evil — then his body becomes the place where offenses gather, as water returns to the sea, gradually growing deep and vast. If a person has faults and immediately knows that they are wrong, and so reforms evil and practices good, the offenses naturally vanish, as a sick person sweats and gradually recovers.

Whether one repents or not — this is the turning point of ascent and fall, the watershed between the common and the holy. We should always be vigilant, courageous in correcting faults, and skillful in correcting faults!

The Buddha said: “When an evil person hears of goodness and deliberately comes to disturb you, you should restrain yourself and have no anger or reproach; the one who comes to do evil brings evil upon himself.”

When an evil person hears that you are practicing goodness, he deliberately comes to disrupt and cause trouble. Against such unreasonable provocation, you should still the discontent in your mind, neither angering nor reproaching him. In this way, he seeks to defile you, but what is defiled is himself.
This is the wondrous method of overcoming evil with goodness.

blocks.text: Chapter 7: Evil Returns to Its Own Body

inline.s: The Buddha said: “There was a person who heard that I uphold the Way and practice great loving-kindness, so he came and reviled the Buddha. The Buddha was silent and did not respond. When the reviling ceased, the Buddha asked: ‘If you offer a gift to a man and he does not accept it, does the gift return to you?’ He replied: ‘It returns!’ The Buddha said: ‘Now you revile me, and I do not accept it; you bear the misfortune yourself and it returns upon your own body! Like an echo answering a sound, like a shadow following a form, one can never escape it. Take care not to do evil.’”

There was a person who heard that the Buddha firmly upheld the bodhi path and practiced great loving-kindness to save living beings, so he came to revile the Buddha. The Buddha remained silent and did not respond. When the man had exhausted his abuse and stopped, the Buddha asked him: “You give a gift to a man, and he does not accept it — does the gift return to you?” The man answered: “Yes, it returns.” Then the Buddha said: “Now you revile me, and I do not accept it; all these curses will be manifested upon your own body!” All curses against others return to oneself, just as an echo answers a sound and a shadow follows a form, without the slightest error. So do not curse others.

When ordinary people are reviled, they all glare back in anger, and even repay abuse with more abuse. But the Buddha not only remained calm and composed; he also explained the principle that “those who do evil to others only harm themselves” and admonished him to beware of bringing harm upon himself, so as to remove the source of his calamity. How incomparable is the Buddha’s compassion!

blocks.text: Chapter 8: Dust and Spittle Defile Only Oneself

inline.s: The Buddha said: “An evil person harming a sage is like spitting upward at the sky — the spittle does not reach the sky but falls back upon himself; or like casting dust against the wind — the dust does not reach the other but falls back and covers his own body. The sage cannot be defamed; the calamity will surely destroy oneself.”

An evil person harming a sage is like looking up and spitting — the spittle cannot reach heaven but falls back on his own face; or like raising dust against the wind — the dust cannot reach ahead but stains his own body. One must not slander sages and saints, because the calamity brought by slandering them will inevitably destroy oneself.
[Ben (
bèn
)] dust; used here as a verb.

blocks.text: Chapter 9: Guarding the Resolve and Fulfilling the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: “One who is broadly learned and loves the Way will find the Way difficult to comprehend; but one who guards his resolve and practices the Way will find the Way great indeed.”

One who reads widely in the sutras and commentaries and loves the Way cannot comprehend the Way; only by single-mindedly and steadfastly practicing the Way can one understand that this is the great Way!

The Buddha’s Dharma is the great Way that severs afflictions, destroys ignorance, and realizes nirvana. If one merely reads, writes, and lectures about it without practicing as it teaches, then one is necessarily working among names and forms and making essays out of subtle words — how could one ever comprehend what the Buddha’s Dharma is (“the Way is difficult to comprehend”)?
[Names and marks] The Buddhist terms and expressions are called “names and marks.”

To love the Way through broad learning yet not guard one’s resolve and practice it — this is the most regrettable thing. For “loving the Way” has already taken the most valuable first step, and “broad learning” shows that one already has the ability to choose the Dharma. Now one need only select the method most suited to oneself and practice it steadfastly and single-mindedly (guarding the resolve and fulfilling the Way), and one has set foot on the golden path.

blocks.text: Chapter 10: Rejoicing in Giving Attains Blessings

inline.s: The Buddha said: “When one sees a person give of the Way and rejoices in helping him, the merit gained is very great. A monk asked: ‘Is this merit exhausted?’ The Buddha said: ‘It is like the flame of one torch — when thousands and hundreds of people each come with their torches to take a share of the fire, to cook food and dispel darkness, this torch remains as before; so too is the merit.’”

Seeing another person spread the Dharma and rejoicing with him — this rejoicing (anumodana) brings very great merit. A monk asked: “If many rejoice, and each person gains great merit, will the merit of spreading the Dharma not be exhausted by them?” The Buddha answered: “No. The merit of spreading the Dharma is like the fire of a single torch. When thousands and hundreds of people come with torches to light their own flames and use this fire to cook food and dispel darkness, the fire that has lit thousands and hundreds of torches remains just as before. So too is the merit of spreading the Dharma.”
[Du] An archaic form of the character “du” (to see).

The Buddha said: “Feeding a hundred evil persons is not equal to feeding one good person; feeding a thousand good persons is not equal to feeding one who upholds the five precepts; feeding ten thousand precept-holders is not equal to feeding one stream-enterer; feeding a million stream-enterers is not equal to feeding one once-returner; feeding ten million once-returners is not equal to feeding one non-returner; feeding a hundred million non-returners is not equal to feeding one arhat; feeding a billion arhats is not equal to feeding one pratyekabuddha; feeding ten billion pratyekabuddhas is not equal to feeding one of the Buddhas of the three times; feeding a hundred billion Buddhas of the three times is not equal to feeding one who has no thought, no abiding, no practice, and no realization.”

Offering food to a hundred evil persons is not as good as offering to one good person; offering food to a thousand good persons is not as good as offering to one precept-holder; offering food to ten thousand precept-holders is not as good as offering to one stream-enterer; offering food to a million stream-enterers is not as good as offering to one once-returner; offering food to ten million once-returners is not as good as offering to one non-returner; offering food to a hundred million non-returners is not as good as offering to one arhat; offering food to a billion arhats is not as good as offering to one pratyekabuddha; offering food to ten billion pratyekabuddhas is not as good as offering to one of the Buddhas of the three times; offering food to a hundred billion Buddhas of the three times is not as good as offering to one who has no thought, no abiding, no practice, and no realization.
Here the Buddha especially emphasizes the supremacy of no-thought, no-abiding, no-practice, no-realization (the unconditioned Dharma).
[Feed] To offer with food and drink.
To make the text easier to understand, some terms need explanation. Readers familiar with these terms may pass over them.

[Small Vehicle] The method of the shravaka (voice-hearer) and the pratyekabuddha, with the aim of self-cultivation and self-benefit. [Two Vehicles] The Shravaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. [Three Vehicles] The Small, Middle, and Great Vehicles. The Small Vehicle is the Shravaka Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle is the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Great Vehicle is the Bodhisattva Vehicle. [Great Vehicle] The method of the bodhisattva, aimed at saving the world and benefiting others; its highest fruit is Buddhahood. The Great Vehicle, from a common person to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages. “Vehicle” means conveyance; it is a metaphor that the Dharma is like a ferry-boat that carries living beings from this shore of birth and death to the other shore of nirvana. The Bodhisattva Vehicle ferries many living beings, hence it is called the Great Vehicle; the Shravaka Vehicle and Pratyekabuddha Vehicle ferry few, hence they are called the Small Vehicle. [Shravaka Vehicle] One who hears the Buddha’s voice and cultivates the method of the four truths and thereby realizes the Way. The Shravaka Vehicle has four fruits: stream-enterer (first fruit), once-returner (second fruit), non-returner (third fruit), and arhat (fourth fruit). Attaining arhatship, one transcends birth and death and leaves the three realms. [Pratyekabuddha Vehicle] One who cultivates the twelve links of dependent origination; its highest fruit is the pratyekabuddha fruit. From a common person to a pratyekabuddha, the practice emphasizes awakening and realization; wherever one awakens is wherever one realizes, so there are no evident stages to be spoken of.

blocks.text: Chapter 12: Enumerating the Difficulties to Urge Practice

inline.s: The Buddha said: “For people there are twenty difficulties. To give when poor is difficult; to study the Way when noble and wealthy is difficult; to cast off one’s life and face death is difficult; to see the Buddha’s scriptures is difficult; to be born in an age when the Buddha appears is difficult; to withstand the temptations of beauty and desire is difficult; to see what is desirable and not seek it is difficult; to be insulted without anger is difficult; to have power and not misuse it is difficult; to be unmoved by matters one encounters is difficult; to study broadly and investigate deeply is difficult; to destroy pride and self-conceit is difficult; not to slight the unlearned is difficult; to practice the mind with equal regard is difficult; not to speak of right and wrong is difficult; to meet a good spiritual friend is difficult; to see one’s nature and study the Way is difficult; to save and transform living beings according to circumstances is difficult; to see states without the mind being moved is difficult; to be skilled in expedient means is difficult.”

There are twenty things very hard for people to do, called the twenty difficulties: for the poor to give alms; for the noble and wealthy to study the Way; to sacrifice one’s life to face death; to see the Buddha’s scriptures; to live in an age when the Buddha is present; to resist the temptation of beauty and desire; to see what one likes and not pursue it; to be insulted without anger; to have power and not abuse it; to encounter matters with an unmoved mind; to study widely and investigate deeply; to destroy pride and arrogance; not to look down on the unlearned; to practice the mind with equal regard and without discrimination; not to speak of right and wrong; to meet a good spiritual friend; to see one’s own nature and study the Way; to teach and save living beings according to conditions and one’s share; to see states without the mind being moved; to be skilled in the expedient means of teaching each person accordingly.
Here the Buddha enumerates the twenty difficulties as an exhortation.

[Good spiritual friend] One who can teach living beings to stay away from evil dharmas and practice the right Dharma. [To see one’s nature and study the Way is difficult] It is easy to study and practice on the level of phenomena and marks, but hard to see one’s own nature and study the Way. Yet to see one’s nature and study the Way is in truth the perfect and sudden method. Master Ouyi said: “Without seeing the true nature of the present single thought of mind, one can never learn the supreme Way” (from the Explanation of the Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters). [Original nature] That is what the Chan school calls one’s original face.

A monk asked the Buddha: “By what causes and conditions can one know past lives and comprehend the ultimate Way?” The Buddha said: “Purify the mind and guard the resolve, and you can comprehend the ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the dust is gone, clarity remains. Sever desire and seek nothing, and you will obtain the knowledge of past lives.”

A monk asked the Buddha: “By what kind of causes and conditions can one obtain the spiritual power of knowing past lives, and come to understand and penetrate the supreme Way?” The Buddha answered: “Purify the mind and guard the resolve, and you can comprehend the ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the dust is gone, clarity remains. Sever desire and seek nothing, remove the dust of the mind, and the innate spiritual powers will naturally manifest; you will obtain the knowledge of past lives.”

[Knowledge of past lives] The spiritual power that knows the lives of past existences and what one did in them; it is one of the six spiritual powers. [Ultimate Way] The supreme Way, that is, the One Buddha Vehicle. [One Buddha Vehicle] The single teaching that can lead one to Buddhahood. [Purify the mind] To remove the distinctions of emotion and consciousness.
